I don't think people should necessarily be let go for distasteful speech, and when that speech was a long time ago it's far less meaningful, and I think that transient Internet outrage is a terrible metric to use to determine how offensive that person's speech actually is. I also think that using it once only primes people to escalate it and use it again and again, which is why we're even at this point where literal mobs are ruining people's lives, and their employers are scared so shitless of the ramifications if they stand up to the thronging masses that they'll bend over backwards--their loyalties, after all, are only to their shareholders, not the people whose lives are being ruined.

Also, if the people acting outraged are the same people who claim to practice tolerance and acceptance, but it's clear from their past behavior that they don't actually practice this, their outrage should be weighted less. A liar's words shouldn't be given equal footing with a truly virtuous person's. We seem to believe that only a person's level of emotion is what matters, rather than that person's character and past deeds.

Consider this: if someone was employed by a small business owner and he knew the employee personally, and a mob of people said that ten years ago he said such-and-such, generally speaking the honorable thing for the owner to do would be to defend his employee. At worst say "I'll handle my business privately, thanks for bringing it to my attention." Firing him within hours would be a coward's response, even if the allegations were true--because a few hours isn't sufficient time to get the other side of the story and let your employee defend himself, nor is it enough time to judge how real the outrage is. And massive allegations, like that your employee sends actual pedophilic messages online, require even more scrutiny.

I'm not proposing a mechanism by which these things can be enforced, but I am judging people's actions relative to the above, which I think would be a better and more rational situation than what we have now.
